item.title: Holiday travel highlights China's transport strength
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Holiday travel highlights China's transport strength For Zhang Yang and his family in Ankang, Northwest China's Shaanxi province, this year's National Day holiday was a memorable one. On Oct 1, following the opening of the Xi'an-Ankang high-speed railway, they took a direct high-speed train from Ankang to Yan'an, a city known for its revolutionary history. The journey, which once took more than seven hours, now takes just over two hours. The Zhang family was among millions on the move during the National Day holiday from Oct 1 to 7, one of China's peak periods for travel and spending. Data from the Ministry of Transport showed cross-regional passenger trips exceeded 300 million on each of the first three days of the holiday. China State Railway Group said the country's railways handled over 25.2 million passenger trips on Oct 1, setting a new single-day record. For a country as vast as China, moving hundreds of millions of people during a holiday rush is a feat of scale. Behind this feat lies a transport network built up over decades. By the end of 2025, China's comprehensive transport network spanned more than 6 million kilometers, including the world's largest high-speed rail network. High-speed railways, expressways, airports and ports connect cities, towns and rural areas across the country. The network continues to expand. On Sept 28, China opened four major high-speed railway sections across northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, with a combined length of more than 1,100 km. The new lines have shortened travel time and put more destinations within easy reach of families like Zhang's. China's transport development goes beyond faster journeys. Better supporting services are also making travel more convenient. New energy vehicles have become increasingly common among Chinese households and are now a popular choice for long-distance travel. The Ministry of Transport expects NEV trips on expressways during the holiday to reach 1.8 times the usual level, pushing up demand for charging services.

item.title: Insured robots becoming irreversible wave
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Insured robots becoming irreversible wave Flexible policies cover design defects, errors in installation, operation; serve as hedge against any financial losses At the China International Fair for Trade in Services in Beijing, which wrapped up on Sept 13, a robotic hand came equipped with an unusual accessory — an insurance policy. The Y-Hand M2, which is designed to mimic the dexterity of a human hand, has added insurance to its working essentials. Its developer — Beijing-based Yue Quan Bionics Ltd — signed an insurance agreement with China Pacific Insurance (Group) Co's property and casualty arm during the event, providing coverage for the hand and any losses it may cause. The idea is straightforward. "If an accident or natural disaster damages the hand while it is being used or stored, the policy provides coverage. It also covers losses caused by defects in design, installation or materials, or by operator error," said Zhou Ai, a staff member at the insurer's Beijing branch. The protection reaches beyond the hand itself. It also includes injuries to third parties or damage to their property during use, Zhou said, adding that the product acts as an industry first for key components of embodied intelligent robots. Behind the paperwork lies a familiar worry for anyone buying expensive high-tech equipment — what happens if it breaks? Especially with humanoid robots and other emerging forms of physical AI that carry out real-world interactions with humans, the concern also extends beyond the machine itself to the people and property around it. In fact, insurers are beginning to offer answers, with coverage for individual components, rented machines and robots whose original warranties have expired. When warranties expire The problem begins with parts that wear out and warranties that run their course. "The core precision components of intelligent robots wear relatively quickly (compared with other physical AI end products), while manufacturers' warranties are limited," said Chen Jian, head of the technology insurance subcenter at PICC Property and Casualty Co's Beijing branch. "Once equipment is out of warranty, repairs and replacement parts are expensive, which to some extent constrains the industry's expansion and commercialization," Chen said. Established last month, Beijing's intelligent robot insurance consortium is designed to address that gap. Gathering PICC's Beijing branch and several other insurers, its first policy focuses on equipment breakdowns after the manufacturer's original warranty expires, providing services including repair and replacement protection. For a manufacturer, the arrangement can support an extended-warranty promise without leaving it to shoulder all the uncertainty over future repairs. For the customer, it helps address the cost of keeping the machine in service after the original guarantee has ended, Chen said. "It helps robot manufacturers ease the financial pressure and operating risks of extended warranties, improve after-sales services and make their products more competitive," he said. "It also helps buyers using the robots allay maintenance concerns, lower the cost of trial applications and accelerate the deployment of robot technology in practical settings." The account puts after-sales support at the center of the insurance proposition: manufacturers need to maintain what they sell, while customers need confidence that a malfunction will not leave them facing an unaffordable repair or replacement. Insurance by the day For businesses that need a robot for a particular assignment rather than a permanent addition to their operations, renting offers a way to put the technology to work without committing to a purchase. Insurance is thus beginning to accommodate that flexibility, with policies tailored to shorter engagements and machines that move between customers. For example, China Pacific Insurance (Group) Co's Jizhibao product, designed for commercial humanoid robot applications, allows customers to purchase coverage by the day, week or month, aligning the period of protection with the length of an assignment. In another way, PICC has worked with robot rental platform Sharebot since December 2025 to offer coverage for damage to machines along with third-party liability, with no fixed operating address within the Chinese mainland mandated in the policy — a provision that accommodates robots moving between customers and venues. The commercial opportunity is backed by substantial market performance. According to iiMedia Research, China's robot rental market stood at about 1 billion yuan ($149 million) in 2025 and is expected to top 10 billion yuan this year, representing an annual growth rate exceeding 900 percent. For rental operators serving this market, the economics of each booking depend partly on managing the repair bills and liability claims that an accident could bring.

item.title: Chinese design takes new form at LA museum
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Chinese design takes new form at LA museum The opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has added a new cultural landmark to Los Angeles, bringing together film, illustration, comics, murals, architecture and landscape while creating a new space for cross-cultural exchange. Founded by filmmaker George Lucas, creator of Star Wars, and his wife, Mellody Hobson, the museum opened to the public last month with a sold-out first day. Designed by Chinese architect Ma Yansong, founder of MAD Architects, the 28,000-square-meter museum traces visual storytelling across cultures and centuries, from cave paintings to cinema and murals. For Ma, the project also represents an opportunity to bring ideas rooted in Chinese architectural tradition to a major United States cultural institution. He conceived the building as a "floating cloud", allowing the landscape and public space to flow beneath it rather than placing a conventional architectural box in the middle of the park. Ma said his approach was influenced by contemporary technology, traditional Chinese gardens, and his childhood experience in Beijing, where lakes, gardens and buildings coexist closely. "As a Chinese architect, I'm really influenced by traditional Chinese architecture, for example, gardens," he said. "The future building should be something new. You don't repeat the wood structure, the sloping roof, but you should continue to create space, connect to nature, to human emotion." He said the idea travels across cultures because the relationship between people and nature is universal. "When I bring this idea to the US or Europe, people love it because nature is a universal topic," Ma said. "Traditional Chinese architecture already talked about this … about emotion and spirituality. It's beyond sustainable and environmental concerns." For Ma, the Lucas Museum became a way to demonstrate that architectural traditions from China can inform a contemporary global design language without simply reproducing historical forms. The museum calls Ma's design a form of "emotional architecture", blurring the boundary between building and park and encouraging visitors to experience the architecture before entering the galleries. The cross-cultural collaboration also extends to the museum's artistic mission. "I've spent more than 50 years collecting the work of artists who don't always get their due — illustrators, cartoonists, muralists, painters — because I believe their images are as vital as any other art form," Lucas said at the opening. "They deserve to be in a museum." The permanent collection holds more than 40,000 works, while the inaugural exhibitions feature more than 1,300 pieces across media and historical periods. The galleries place popular and fine art in the same narrative tradition, bringing together artists such as Norman Rockwell, Frida Kahlo, Robert Colescott, Frank Frazetta and Robert Crumb with film materials from the Lucas Archives. Ryan Linkof, senior curator and head of film programs at the museum, said China offered many avenues for exploration. "As such an important part of world culture, China would of course be a place where we could find all kinds of avenues to explore," he said. "Certainly, going forward, we have a lot of opportunities for that." For visitors, the blend of architecture and art is already part of the experience. Adira Vasquez, who attended the opening, described the building as both modern and futuristic, saying its curving profile sharply contrasts with the nearby Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. "You see a sports stadium there, it's very iconic, the LA Coliseum, and then you turn, and you see this little piece of art of architecture right next to it," she said. renali@chinadailyusa.com

item.title: Chinese AI models see intl adoption surge
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Chinese AI models see intl adoption surge Shift from winning attention to selling through major global platforms lauded United States-based cloud computing giant Amazon Web Services said on Tuesday that it has made GLM-5.3, the latest flagship model from China's Z.ai, available on the Amazon Bedrock platform, while sources familiar with the matter confirmed that AWS would share revenue with Z.ai based on the usage of the model. Industry experts said the move underscores a broader shift in the global expansion of Chinese artificial intelligence models: from winning attention among overseas developers to gaining real-world adoption, while increasingly being sold through major international commercial platforms. Z.ai is not alone. AWS has added six open-weight Chinese models, including DeepSeek V3.2, MiniMax M2.1 and Alibaba's Qwen3 Coder Next, into the Amazon Bedrock platform. In September, Moonshot's Kimi K3 also became available on Amazon Bedrock. According to Wang Peng, a researcher with Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, such a shift means that each genuine overseas model call would now be converted into commercial revenue. Wang said that under the cloud revenue-sharing approach, open models help build a developer ecosystem, global cloud computing companies provide computing infrastructure and access to corporate customers, and model developers receive a share of the income generated when customers actually use their models. "A year ago, the overseas expansion of Chinese models was largely about getting foreign developers to use them. Now, an increasingly clear shift is taking place: overseas commercial platforms are starting to actively sell them," Wang said. Latest data from AI model aggregation platform OpenRouter showed that Chinese models processed about 57.46 trillion tokens in the week ending Sunday, compared with about 16.2 trillion tokens by US models. It was the 23rd consecutive week in which Chinese models had higher weekly token usage than US models on the platform. DeepSeek alone accounted for 21.8 percent of text requests in Open-Router's latest full week, while Z.ai and Qwen were also among its biggest model providers. Another indicator came from Hugging Face, the world's largest open-source AI community. Its report showed that Chinese-developed models accounted for about 41 percent of model downloads on the platform over the previous year, surpassing those from the US. By this summer, Alibaba's Qwen model family had recorded about 2.045 billion downloads on Hugging Face, while the number of derivative models built on Qwen had reached 151,448, about 2.6 times the total number of derivatives based on Meta's models from the US. Zhang Yaqin, founding dean of Tsinghua University's Institute for AI Industry Research and a foreign member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said: "Openness could become a structural advantage for China's AI industry. Lower costs and easier access have made models such as DeepSeek and Qwen particularly attractive to smaller companies and emerging markets." Wang from the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences noted that the global rollout of Chinese AI models helps diversify the global AI landscape and reduces reliance on a small number of technology players. "These models lower barriers to AI adoption, offer cost-effective solutions for overseas businesses and inject fresh momentum into the global digital economy. Open-source collaboration and open sharing can also promote more inclusive global AI development and help build a more diverse, balanced AI ecosystem." Shen Yang, a professor at Tsinghua University, said: "Chinese AI companies were already encountering different market conditions as they expanded overseas. Southeast Asia offered relatively strong commercial certainty, Gulf markets had higher value per customer, while Latin America had significant unmet demand." Foreign countries are also increasingly pursuing their own forms of "AI sovereignty", Shen said. Contact the writers at chengyu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Two scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry STOCKHOLM -- Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Wednesday. According to the Academy, some molecules, such as amino acids, exist in two variants that are mirror images of each other. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror-image forms. How such chemical asymmetry, known as homochirality, could emerge had long remained a mystery to chemists. "This year's prize recognises discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality," the Academy said in a statement, noting that the two laureates "made chemistry choose a mirror image." "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," says Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry. Kagan, born in France on Dec 15, 1930, is affiliated with Universite Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, born in Japan in 1950, is a professor at Tokyo University of Science.

item.title: A Spanish envoy's lifelong journey in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Inma Gonzalez Puy of Barcelona has for decades been living in China and fostering connections between Spain and China. Therefore, it is with some conviction that the director of the Cervantes Institute in Beijing says, "Cultures are one of the most powerful tools for connecting different societies." The Barcelona native's connection with China began not with a plane ticket but with a book. In her teenage years, she stumbled upon Spanish translations of works by Pearl S. Buck and Lin Yutang — writers who painted vivid images of a country she had never seen. "In the 1970s Spain, books about China were scarce. Yet those few volumes sparked a deep curiosity about a distant and mysterious land. In a way, they were what set me on this journey to China," she recalls. That journey became reality in 1979, when Beijing began recruiting international students from Spain for the first time. Gonzalez Puy, then a university student, seized the opportunity and applied to study at the Beijing Language Institute — now Beijing Language and Culture University. "Those readings opened the first imaginary door to China for me," she says. "Later, when I arrived in 1979, I discovered a reality far more complex and captivating than any literary depiction." Her studies cemented her resolve to live in China. In 1983, Gonzalez Puy returned to work at the Spanish embassy in Beijing, where she would spend 20 years — first as a translator, then as cultural attache. "Those were pivotal years for the consolidation of bilateral ties, and my professional career unfolded almost in lockstep with contemporary China's transformation," she says. "Those years convinced me that culture is not merely a supplementary element of diplomacy, but one of its most profound instruments. An exhibition, a book or a film can open pathways of understanding that endure for generations." Throughout her career, Gonzalez Puy has championed this belief through tangible projects. In 1995, she curated a groundbreaking exhibition of Chinese avant-garde art in Barcelona, introducing more than 30 Chinese contemporary artists to a European audience.

item.title: Take me home, county roads
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Take me home, county roads More tourists from cities going off the beaten track in search of raw places, authentic experiences and a slow-paced life Standing atop Chijia Mountain above the Yangtze River in Chongqing's Fengjie county, known as Kuizhou during the Tang Dynasty (618-907), Chen Xiangying finally understood why Du Fu, the great poet, produced hundreds of poems despite spending only about a year and nine months there. She had not come merely as a sightseer, but as a reader, following the geography of classical Chinese poetry. Chen, a 39-year-old university lecturer in ancient literature from Yan'an, Shaanxi province, said the experience of visiting the places she had read about was completely different from reading about them in books. "When I actually got there, I felt very different. Du Fu's poems suddenly appeared in front of me. He wrote, 'The Chijia and Baiyan peaks rise, both piercing the sky'. And then I understood why Du Fu wrote those poems," Chen said. Chen's experience is part of a broader shift in China's domestic tourism market, as growing numbers of urban residents turn away from megacities and popular ancient towns and toward county-level destinations in search of unpolished landscapes, living cultural memories and a slower pace of life. In August, Chen and a friend traveled to Fengjie and Wushan counties in Chongqing. "They're small counties, but the cultural accumulation is incredibly deep. Not only Du Fu, but also poets like Li Bai and Bai Juyi passed through and wrote about them," she said. What also moved her was the sense of stepping out of time. "The streets still look like the 1990s or the early 2000s. In a second you're back in childhood. It's completely different from Shanghai or Beijing. Here, you can still see the past, including old restaurants, old buildings and places with stories." In the counties, Chen noticed that the ride-hailing drivers she met seemed genuinely content. "They were not exhausted, not like drivers in big cities. One driver warmly shared some local knowledge with us and gave us a glimpse into everyday life in the area," she said. "Small restaurant owners worked briskly and cheerfully. We'd watch what locals ordered and order the same." But county rhythms are not urban rhythms. If visitors miss the meal window, there may be no food available. The famous local buns, for example, were sold out by 9 am, she said. "I had a wonderful time, and I ate very well. It's worth going, not because food and lodging are cheap, but because the experience is real." She was also impressed by the way the Wushan Museum presents local history.

item.title: Desert oasis a lifeline for migratory birds
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Desert oasis a lifeline for migratory birds Protected Gansu wetlands a 'natural breeding ground' for black storks, other species For nearly three months, a young black stork stayed in its nest on a cliff in Gansu province, waiting to learn how to fly. Then the time came for the nestling to leave its temporary home in Gaotai county, Zhangye. Other chicks in the same nest had already flown off. But the third, whose leg had been broken, remained behind. Documentary filmmaker Zhao Hai remembered the scene while watching footage captured by an infrared camera near the nest. The young bird hesitated to leave the nest, while its parents stayed nearby. Eventually, the chick took off. Its parents flew alongside it for a while, as if encouraging it on its first flight. For Zhao, who has observed birds for about 30 years and filmed them for more than two decades, it was one of many moments that have made black storks more than a subject for his camera. "When we watch birds, sometimes their behavior is basically the same as that of humans," he said. He recalled another touching scene. When newly hatched black stork chicks were still tiny and April mornings and evenings could be cold, an adult bird brought pieces of plastic to the nest and covered the chicks with them. "It was almost like covering the chicks with a blanket to keep them warm," Zhao said. Such moments are difficult to capture. Black storks are highly wary of people, and Zhao has tried to minimize disturbing them while filming. So far, he has filmed two nests through most of the breeding process. But what he has seen at the nests is part of a much larger story unfolding along the Zhangye Heihe Wetland.

item.title: Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade unveils medals, torch
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade unveils medals, torch Share - WeChat
CHANGCHUN - Medals, the torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event at Changchun International Aviation Expo City. The torch, named "Ji Xiang," or "Auspicious Flight," is inspired by the clivia, Changchun's city flower. Its upper section features a filmstrip motif and 12 winter sports icons representing the Games' disciplines, a reference to Changchun's film industry. Snowflake and ginseng flower motifs appear near the top, while ski-inspired lines run down the sides and a wheel-hub pattern decorates the base. The torch stands 711 millimeters tall, a reference to the highest elevation in Changchun's urban area, 711 meters.

item.title: Visionary Pathway: The Enduring Voice of Minju Opera
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Visionary Pathway: The Enduring Voice of Minju Opera Share - WeChat
For more than four centuries, Minju Opera has been part of Fuzhou's cultural identity. But in the 1980s, the art form faced a fight for survival. Xi Jinping, who served as Party secretary of Fuzhou from 1990 to 1996, championed a series of measures to preserve it — from securing stable funding for theater troupes to establishing a dedicated training school. Today, thanks to decades of sustained efforts, the ancient art form has found new life and continues to inspire new generations.
